af.about: A landlocked, mountainous country at the crossroads of Central and South Asia, wedged between Iran, Pakistan and the former Soviet republics. About 40 million people speak Dari and Pashto. The modern state dates from the Durrani Empire of 1747; it later served as a buffer in the Anglo-Russian Great Game and won full independence in 1919. A Soviet invasion in 1979 began four decades of war: civil conflict, Taliban rule, a US-led intervention in 2001, and the Taliban's return in 2021. It is now an Islamic emirate under Taliban control.
known: Hindu Kush mountains and Khyber Pass

ax.about: An autonomous and demilitarised archipelago of Finland in the Baltic Sea, between Sweden and the Finnish mainland. Its roughly 30,000 inhabitants are Swedish-speaking and govern themselves through their own parliament, the Lagting, with their own flag and stamps. The islands passed from Sweden to Russia with Finland in 1809 and were demilitarised after the Crimean War. When Finland became independent, Ålanders asked to join Sweden; the League of Nations awarded them to Finland in 1921 with guaranteed autonomy. They joined the EU with Finland in 1995 but stay outside its tax area.
dates: Ceded by Sweden to Russia with Finland
League of Nations grants autonomy under Finland

al.about: A small Balkan country on the Adriatic and Ionian coasts, bordered by Montenegro, Kosovo, North Macedonia and Greece. About 2.8 million people speak Albanian, a language with no close relatives. It is a parliamentary republic, a NATO member and an EU candidate. Descended from the ancient Illyrians, it spent nearly five centuries under Ottoman rule before independence in 1912. After Italian occupation in the Second World War, Enver Hoxha built one of the most isolated communist regimes anywhere, dotting the country with bunkers. Communism collapsed in 1991, followed by a rocky transition.

dz.about: The largest country in Africa, stretching from the Mediterranean deep into the Sahara, which covers most of its territory. About 45 million people live mainly along the coast; Arabic and Berber are official and French is widely used. A presidential republic in which the army is highly influential, it earns most of its income from oil and gas. Home to Numidian kingdoms and Roman cities, it was later an Ottoman regency before France conquered it in 1830 and settled it heavily. A brutal war of independence ended in 1962; a civil war against Islamist insurgents scarred the 1990s.
known: Roman ruins of Timgad and Djémila

as.about: An unincorporated territory of the United States in the South Pacific, comprising the eastern islands of the Samoan archipelago, chiefly Tutuila with its deep harbour at Pago Pago. About 45,000 people speak Samoan and English; they are US nationals rather than citizens and elect their own governor and legislature. Settled by Polynesians some three thousand years ago, Samoa was divided between Germany and the United States in 1899. The US Navy ran the eastern islands until 1951, when civilian administration took over. Traditional chiefly culture, fa'a Samoa, remains strong.
dates: Samoa divided between US and Germany

ad.about: A tiny landlocked principality high in the Pyrenees between France and Spain. About 80,000 people live in its valleys, with Catalan as the official language. Its unusual form of government is a co-principality: the heads of state are the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain, a system dating back to a 1278 treaty, while a constitution adopted in 1993 made it a parliamentary democracy. Long poor and isolated, Andorra prospered in the twentieth century on duty-free shopping, skiing and banking. It is not an EU member but uses the euro.
dates: Consell de la Terra, early parliament, founded
First constitution; joins the United Nations
known: Co-princes: French president and a bishop

ao.about: A large country on the Atlantic coast of south-western Africa, bordered by the two Congos, Zambia and Namibia, with the oil-rich exclave of Cabinda to the north. About 36 million people speak Portuguese and Bantu languages. It is a presidential republic ruled by the MPLA since independence. The Portuguese founded Luanda in 1575 and the colony became a major source of enslaved people for Brazil. Independence in 1975 was followed immediately by a 27-year civil war between the MPLA and UNITA. Since peace in 2002, oil and diamonds have driven growth amid stark inequality.
dates: Independence from Portugal; civil war begins
Civil war ends after Savimbi's death
Dos Santos steps down after 38 years
known: Luanda, once among world's costliest cities

ai.about: A British Overseas Territory in the eastern Caribbean, a flat, dry coral island just north of Saint Martin. Its roughly 15,000 English-speaking inhabitants run their own internal affairs under a UK-appointed governor. Settled by the English in 1650, Anguilla was for centuries administered together with Saint Kitts, an arrangement islanders resented. In 1967 they rebelled, expelled the Kittitian police and declared independence; British paratroopers landed in 1969 and the island was formally separated in 1980. Today it lives on luxury tourism and offshore finance.
dates: Revolt against union with Saint Kitts
British forces land to restore order

ag.about: A twin-island nation in the Leeward Islands of the eastern Caribbean, with most of its roughly 100,000 English-speaking people on Antigua; Barbuda is low, sparsely settled and wildlife-rich. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state. Colonised by the English in 1632, Antigua became a sugar island worked by enslaved Africans and the base of Britain's Caribbean fleet at Nelson's Dockyard. Independence came in 1981. Tourism now dominates the economy; Hurricane Irma devastated Barbuda in 2017.
known: A beach for every day of the year

ar.about: The second-largest country in South America, running from the subtropical north through the Pampas grasslands to Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego, with the Andes along its border with Chile. About 46 million people speak Spanish; it is a federal presidential republic. A Spanish colony, it declared independence in 1816 and, after civil wars, drew millions of European immigrants to become one of the world's richest countries by 1900. The twentieth century brought Peronism, military dictatorships, the 1976–83 junta's Dirty War and the Falklands defeat. Democracy returned in 1983, punctuated by recurring economic crises.
dates: Military coup begins the Dirty War

am.about: A small, landlocked, mountainous country in the South Caucasus, bordered by Turkey, Georgia, Azerbaijan and Iran. About 3 million people speak Armenian, written in its own alphabet, and a large diaspora lives abroad. It is a parliamentary republic. Armenia was the first state to adopt Christianity, in 301, and its ancient kingdoms were long contested by Persians, Byzantines, Ottomans and Russians. The 1915 genocide in the Ottoman Empire shaped its modern identity. After seven decades as a Soviet republic it became independent in 1991, then fought Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, losing the region in 2020–23.

aw.about: A small, dry island off the coast of Venezuela and a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, which handles its defence and foreign affairs. About 110,000 people speak Papiamento and Dutch, plus English and Spanish. Claimed by Spain in 1499 and taken by the Dutch in 1636, Aruba stayed a quiet backwater until a huge oil refinery opened in the 1920s. In 1986 it left the Netherlands Antilles to gain separate status within the Kingdom, and later shelved plans for full independence. Tourism, helped by its position outside the hurricane belt, now drives the economy.
dates: Separate status within the Dutch Kingdom

au.about: A continent-sized country between the Indian and Pacific oceans, the sixth-largest in the world, with a vast arid interior and a population of about 27 million concentrated in coastal cities. English-speaking, it is a federal parliamentary democracy and a Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state. Aboriginal peoples have lived here for at least 60,000 years. Britain founded a penal colony at Sydney in 1788; gold rushes brought settlers in the 1850s, and six colonies federated in 1901. Post-war immigration made it multicultural; a 1999 referendum on becoming a republic failed.
known: Sydney Opera House and Harbour Bridge

at.about: A landlocked Alpine country in Central Europe bordering eight countries, including Germany, Italy, Switzerland and Hungary. About 9 million people speak German. It is a federal parliamentary republic, constitutionally neutral since 1955 and an EU member since 1995. For six centuries the Habsburgs ruled from Vienna, heading the Holy Roman Empire and then the vast Austro-Hungarian monarchy, which collapsed in 1918 leaving a small republic. Annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938 and occupied by the Allies after 1945, Austria regained full sovereignty with the State Treaty of 1955 and has since been prosperous and stable.
dates: State Treaty restores independence and neutrality
known: Vienna's palaces, opera and coffee houses
Salzburg and The Sound of Music

az.about: A country in the South Caucasus on the Caspian Sea, bordered by Russia, Georgia, Armenia and Iran, with the exclave of Nakhchivan beyond Armenia. About 10 million people speak Azerbaijani, a Turkic language; most are Shia Muslims in a secular state. It is an authoritarian presidential republic ruled by the Aliyev family since 1993. Russia took the region from Persia in the early 1800s and Baku's oil boom followed. After a brief republic in 1918–20 it was Soviet until 1991. It then lost Nagorno-Karabakh to Armenian forces, but retook the territory in wars of 2020 and 2023.
known: Mud volcanoes and burning hillside Yanar Dag

bs.about: An archipelago of some 700 islands and cays in the Atlantic, south-east of Florida and north of Cuba, with most of its roughly 400,000 English-speaking people on New Providence around Nassau. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state. Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas here in 1492. English settlers arrived in 1648, pirates such as Blackbeard used the islands as a base until Britain imposed order in 1718, and American Loyalists arrived after 1783. Independence came in 1973; tourism and offshore banking dominate the economy.
dates: Columbus's first landfall in the Americas

bh.about: A small island kingdom in the Persian Gulf, linked to Saudi Arabia by the King Fahd Causeway. About 1.5 million people live here, over half of them foreign workers; Arabic is official. It is a monarchy under the Sunni Al Khalifa dynasty, ruling a majority Shia population, with a parliament of limited power. Site of the ancient Dilmun trading civilisation and later a pearling centre, Bahrain was a British protectorate from the nineteenth century and in 1932 found the Gulf's first oil. It became independent in 1971; Arab Spring protests in 2011 were suppressed with Saudi help. Banking has replaced declining oil.
dates: First oil discovered in the Gulf
known: Tree of Life in the desert

bd.about: One of the world's most densely populated countries, occupying the low delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra on the Bay of Bengal, almost entirely surrounded by India. About 170 million people speak Bengali; it is a parliamentary republic. Part of Mughal and British Bengal, it became East Pakistan at partition in 1947, separated from West Pakistan by 1,600 km of India. Resentment, sharpened by the 1952 language movement, led to a bloody independence war in 1971 won with Indian help. Garment exports have fuelled rapid growth since; floods and cyclones remain constant threats. Mass protests ousted Sheikh Hasina in 2024.
dates: Partition of India; becomes East Pakistan

bb.about: The easternmost island of the Caribbean, a flat coral island of about 280,000 English-speaking people. Settled by the English in 1627 and never ruled by anyone else, it became a hugely profitable sugar colony worked by enslaved Africans and was known as Little England for its British ways. Slavery ended in 1834, independence came in 1966, and in 2021 Barbados removed the British monarch to become a parliamentary republic within the Commonwealth. Today it is one of the region's most prosperous societies, living on tourism, finance and rum.

by.about: A landlocked, flat and forested country in Eastern Europe between Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. About 9 million people; Belarusian and Russian are official, with Russian dominant. It is an authoritarian presidential republic ruled by Alexander Lukashenko since 1994 and closely allied with Russia. Its lands belonged to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and Poland before Russia absorbed them in the late 1700s. The Second World War killed a quarter of the population, and the 1986 Chernobyl disaster contaminated the south. Independent since 1991, it saw mass protests after a disputed 2020 election, which were crushed.
dates: Absorbed by Russia in Poland's partition

be.about: A small, densely populated country in Western Europe between France, the Netherlands, Germany and Luxembourg, with a short North Sea coast. About 11.7 million people are divided between Dutch-speaking Flanders, French-speaking Wallonia and bilingual Brussels, plus a small German community; the language divide shapes its politics. It is a federal parliamentary constitutional monarchy and hosts the headquarters of the EU and NATO. Long a battleground of Europe under Burgundian, Spanish and Austrian rule, it broke from the Netherlands in 1830, ruled the Congo brutally, was overrun in both world wars and co-founded the European project.
dates: German invasion in the First World War
known: Brussels, home of EU and NATO
Cycling classics like Tour of Flanders

bz.about: A small country on the Caribbean coast of Central America, bordered by Mexico and Guatemala, with jungle inland and the hemisphere's largest barrier reef offshore. About 400,000 people; English is official, the only such case in Central America, with Spanish and Kriol widely spoken. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm. Once part of the Maya heartland, it was settled by British logwood cutters in the 1600s and became the colony of British Honduras. Renamed Belize in 1973, it gained independence in 1981. Guatemala long claimed its territory; the dispute is now before the International Court of Justice.
dates: Maya city of Caracol at its height
Battle of St George's Caye repels Spain
Hurricane Hattie; capital moved to Belmopan
known: Barrier reef and Great Blue Hole
Maya ruins of Caracol and Xunantunich

bj.about: A narrow West African country on the Gulf of Guinea, between Togo and Nigeria, stretching north to Burkina Faso and Niger. About 13 million people; French is official alongside Fon, Yoruba and others. It is a presidential republic; Porto-Novo is the official capital while government sits in Cotonou. The Kingdom of Dahomey, famous for its female warriors, dominated the coast and the slave trade from the 1600s until France conquered it in 1894. Independent as Dahomey in 1960, it endured coups and a Marxist regime, took the name Benin in 1975, and in 1990 pioneered Africa's wave of democratic transitions.

bm.about: A British Overseas Territory in the North Atlantic about 1,000 km east of the Carolinas, far from the Caribbean despite its tropical image. Some 64,000 people, English-speaking, enjoy one of the world's highest incomes thanks to offshore insurance and reinsurance. Bermuda has had a parliament since 1620, making it Britain's oldest self-governing colony. Uninhabited when sighted by Juan de Bermúdez around 1505, it was settled after the English ship Sea Venture wrecked there in 1609, an event said to have inspired Shakespeare's The Tempest. Voters rejected independence in a 1995 referendum.
dates: Sea Venture wreck brings English settlers

bt.about: A small, landlocked Himalayan kingdom between Tibet and India, rising from subtropical plains to peaks over 7,000 metres. About 800,000 people speak Dzongkha and practise Vajrayana Buddhism. A constitutional monarchy since 2008, it famously measures progress by Gross National Happiness. Unified by a Tibetan lama in the 1600s and ruled by the Wangchuck dynasty since 1907, Bhutan stayed almost sealed off from the world until the 1960s, admitting television and the internet only in 1999. It limits tourism, protects its forests by law and remains one of the few carbon-negative countries.

bo.about: A landlocked country in the heart of South America, from the high Andean altiplano in the west to Amazon lowlands in the east. About 12 million people; Spanish is official alongside Quechua, Aymara and other Indigenous languages. Sucre is the constitutional capital while government sits in La Paz. Heir to Tiwanaku and the Inca, it supplied Spain with Potosí silver, became independent in 1825 and was named after Simón Bolívar. It lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific, saw a 1952 revolution and many coups, and elected its first Indigenous president, Evo Morales, in 2006.
dates: War of the Pacific; loses coastline
known: La Paz, world's highest seat of government

ba.about: A mountainous Balkan country bordered by Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro, with a sliver of Adriatic coast at Neum. About 3.2 million people belong mostly to three groups: Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats, speaking closely related languages. Under the 1995 Dayton Accords it is split into two entities, the Federation and Republika Srpska, with a three-member rotating presidency. A medieval kingdom, it was Ottoman for four centuries, then Austro-Hungarian; the 1914 assassination in Sarajevo triggered the First World War. Its 1992–95 war of independence from Yugoslavia brought siege, ethnic cleansing and the Srebrenica genocide.
dates: Sarajevo assassination sparks First World War
Srebrenica massacre; Dayton Accords end war
known: Mosques, churches and synagogues side by side

bw.about: A landlocked southern African country, mostly covered by the Kalahari, bordered by South Africa, Namibia, Zimbabwe and Zambia. About 2.5 million people; English is official and Setswana widely spoken. A stable parliamentary republic, it has held free elections since independence and is often cited as an African success story. Tswana chiefs sought British protection in 1885 to fend off Boer and German expansion, creating the Bechuanaland Protectorate. Independence came in 1966 under Seretse Khama; diamonds discovered the next year turned one of the world's poorest countries into an upper-middle-income one. The ruling party lost power peacefully in 2024.

br.about: The giant of South America and the world's fifth-largest country, holding most of the Amazon basin and a 7,500 km Atlantic coast. About 215 million people speak Portuguese; it is a federal presidential republic. Claimed by Portugal in 1500, it grew rich on sugar, gold and coffee and received more enslaved Africans than any other country. The Portuguese court fled here from Napoleon, and in 1822 Brazil became an independent empire; it abolished slavery in 1888, the last in the Americas, and became a republic a year later. A military dictatorship ruled from 1964 to 1985; the 1988 constitution underpins today's democracy.
known: Rio Carnival, samba and bossa nova

vg.about: A British Overseas Territory of about sixty islands in the Caribbean east of Puerto Rico, with most of its roughly 30,000 English-speaking people on Tortola. It governs its own internal affairs under a UK-appointed governor and uses the US dollar. The Dutch planted a settlement in 1648 before England annexed Tortola in 1672 and introduced sugar and slavery. After emancipation the islands languished until the 1960s, when tourism and yachting took off, and a 1984 law made them one of the world's biggest registries of offshore companies. Hurricane Irma caused severe damage in 2017.

bn.about: A tiny, oil-rich sultanate on the north coast of Borneo, split into two parts and surrounded by the Malaysian state of Sarawak. About 450,000 people speak Malay; most are Muslim. It is an absolute monarchy under Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, on the throne since 1967 and among the world's longest-reigning monarchs. A powerful empire in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries controlling much of Borneo, Brunei dwindled before becoming a British protectorate in 1888. Oil discovered in 1929 brought great wealth. A revolt in 1962 led to emergency rule still in force; independence came in 1984. A strict sharia penal code was introduced in 2014.
known: Sultan's vast Istana Nurul Iman palace

bg.about: A country in south-eastern Europe on the Black Sea, bordered by Romania, Serbia, North Macedonia, Greece and Turkey and crossed by the Balkan Mountains. About 6.5 million people speak Bulgarian, written in Cyrillic, which was developed here in the ninth century. It is a parliamentary republic, in NATO since 2004 and the EU since 2007, and adopted the euro in 2026. The First Bulgarian Empire of 681 was a medieval great power; five centuries of Ottoman rule ended with liberation in 1878. After fighting on the losing side in both world wars, Bulgaria spent 1946–89 as a loyal Soviet satellite.
known: Rose oil from the Valley of Roses

bf.about: A landlocked country in the West African Sahel, bordered by Mali, Niger, Benin, Togo, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire. About 23 million people; French is official and Mooré the largest local language. Since coups in 2022 it has been run by a military junta that has turned from France toward Russia and left ECOWAS with Mali and Niger, while fighting a jihadist insurgency that controls much of the countryside. The Mossi kingdoms ruled here from medieval times until France created the colony of Upper Volta. Independent in 1960, it was renamed Burkina Faso by the revolutionary Thomas Sankara, who was assassinated in 1987.
dates: French colony of Upper Volta created

bi.about: A small, densely populated and landlocked country in Africa's Great Lakes region, bordered by Rwanda, Tanzania and DR Congo along Lake Tanganyika. About 13 million people speak Kirundi; French and English are also official. A presidential republic, it moved its capital from Bujumbura to Gitega in 2019 and is among the world's poorest countries. A kingdom from the 1600s, it passed from German to Belgian rule as part of Ruanda-Urundi and became independent in 1962. Tensions between the Hutu majority and Tutsi minority produced mass killings in 1972 and a civil war from 1993 to 2005.
known: Claimed southernmost source of the Nile

kh.about: A South-East Asian country on the Gulf of Thailand, bordered by Thailand, Laos and Vietnam and centred on the Mekong and the great Tonlé Sap lake. About 17 million people speak Khmer and are mostly Theravada Buddhist. A constitutional monarchy in form, it has been dominated since the 1980s by Hun Sen's party, with his son Hun Manet prime minister since 2023. The Khmer Empire built Angkor and ruled much of the region from the ninth to fifteenth centuries. A French protectorate from 1863, Cambodia became independent in 1953, then suffered the Khmer Rouge genocide of 1975–79, which killed around two million people.
known: Killing Fields of the Khmer Rouge

cm.about: A Central African country on the Gulf of Guinea, bordered by Nigeria, Chad, the Central African Republic, Congo, Gabon and Equatorial Guinea. Called Africa in miniature for its range of deserts, mountains, rainforest and coast, it has about 28 million people speaking French, English and over 250 local languages. It is a presidential republic ruled by Paul Biya since 1982. A German colony from 1884, it was split between France and Britain after the First World War; the French part became independent in 1960 and the British south joined it in 1961. Since 2017 an Anglophone separatist conflict has troubled the west.

ca.about: The world's second-largest country by area, spanning North America from the Atlantic to the Pacific and far into the Arctic, though most of its roughly 40 million people live within a short drive of the US border. English and French are official; it is a federal parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm of ten provinces and three territories. Home to Indigenous peoples for millennia, it was colonised by France from 1608 and conquered by Britain in 1763. The colonies confederated in 1867, a transcontinental railway bound them together, and full constitutional independence came in 1982. Quebec twice voted against separation (1980, and very narrowly in 1995).
dates: Confederation creates the Dominion of Canada
Constitution patriated with Charter of Rights
known: Maple syrup and the maple leaf

cv.about: An archipelago of ten volcanic islands in the Atlantic, about 570 km off Senegal. Around 550,000 people live here, speaking Portuguese and the Creole language Kriolu, while an even larger diaspora lives abroad. It is a stable multiparty republic, one of Africa's best-governed. Uninhabited until Portuguese settlers arrived in the 1460s, the islands became a hub of the Atlantic slave trade and later suffered devastating droughts and famines. Independence came in 1975 under the party that also freed Guinea-Bissau; plans to unite the two countries were dropped in 1980. Tourism and remittances sustain the economy.
known: Beaches of Sal and Boa Vista

bq.about: Three small Caribbean islands, Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, that have been special municipalities of the Netherlands since the Netherlands Antilles was dissolved in 2010. Bonaire lies off Venezuela; Statia and Saba are in the Leeward Islands near Sint Maarten. Together they have about 30,000 people; Dutch is official, with Papiamento spoken on Bonaire and English on the other two, and the US dollar is the currency. The Dutch took them in the 1630s. Statia, once a bustling free port, fired the first foreign salute to the American flag in 1776. Bonaire is a diving destination; Saba holds the Kingdom's highest point.
dates: Sint Eustatius salutes the American flag
Become special municipalities of the Netherlands
known: Saba's Mount Scenery, Kingdom's highest peak

ky.about: A British Overseas Territory of three islands in the western Caribbean south of Cuba: Grand Cayman, Cayman Brac and Little Cayman. About 80,000 people, English-speaking, enjoy the highest living standard in the Caribbean. It governs itself internally under a UK-appointed governor. Columbus sighted the islands in 1503 and England acquired them with Jamaica in 1670; they were a dependency of Jamaica until it became independent in 1962, when Cayman chose to remain British. From the 1960s a tax-free regime turned it into one of the world's largest financial centres, home to thousands of hedge funds. Hurricane Ivan struck hard in 2004.
